topic: bone and soft tissue lumps — suspected sarcoma referral
page_contents_html:
Bone and soft tissue lumps: assessment and suspected sarcoma referral

Sarcomas are rare but the cost of a missed one is high. The rule of thumb: any soft tissue lump that is >5 cm, deep to fascia, growing, painful or recurrent needs urgent ultrasound; unexplained non-mechanical bone pain needs an X-ray.

  • Suspicious soft tissue lump → urgent ultrasound; suspicious/uncertain scan → urgent suspicion-of-cancer referral to the sarcoma service.
  • Persistent unexplained bone pain at a single site → X-ray plus first-line bloods (mimics: metastasis, myeloma, Paget's). X-ray suggesting bone tumour → urgent discussion/referral — do not biopsy outside the specialist centre.
  • Small, superficial, soft, stable lumps (typical lipomata) and classic wrist ganglia can be managed in primary care.

DRAFT for departmental review. Content based on national guidance (NICE / SIGN / BOA); local routes, thresholds and contact points to be confirmed with the orthopaedic department before publication.

accordion_sections.heading: Background
accordion_sections.html:
Soft tissue sarcomas (~3,300/year UK) and bone sarcomas (~600/year) are rare, and most lumps GPs see are benign (lipomata, ganglia, sebaceous cysts). Outcomes depend on size at diagnosis, and inadvertent excision or biopsy outside a sarcoma centre worsens prognosis — the aim in primary care is recognition and routing, not removal.

Bone sarcomas peak in adolescents and young adults — persistent unexplained bone pain in a teenager deserves an X-ray, and a normal X-ray does not fully exclude it if pain persists.

accordion_sections.heading: Assessment
accordion_sections.html:
Soft tissue lump — features raising suspicion:

  • Size >5 cm (golf ball)
  • Deep to fascia / fixed
  • Increasing in size (the single most important feature)
  • Painful
  • Recurrence after previous excision

Bone — features raising suspicion of sarcoma: persistent unexplained pain at a single site, non-mechanical or night pain, swelling or palpable bony mass, pathological fracture. Age matters: primary bone sarcoma peaks in adolescents and young adults; over 50, metastasis and myeloma are considerably more likely causes of a destructive lesion.

Localised vs generalised bone pain. This pathway concerns pain at a single site. Generalised, multifocal or symmetrical bone pain points to metabolic or haematological disease — osteomalacia, myeloma, widespread metastases, hyperparathyroidism — and needs a bloods-led workup rather than the sarcoma route.

Other causes of localised bone pain — several can present at a single site:

  • Metastasis — the commonest destructive bone lesion over 40 (breast, prostate, lung, renal, thyroid); may be the first presentation of the primary
  • Myeloma / solitary plasmacytoma — can present as a single painful lytic lesion; check myeloma screen (see below) and the myeloma & MGUS pathway
  • Paget's disease — usually >50; isolated raised ALP with normal calcium and phosphate; characteristic X-ray appearance
  • Osteomyelitis — fever, raised inflammatory markers, risk factors (diabetes, recent infection, IVDU)
  • Osteoid osteoma — adolescent/young adult; night pain classically relieved by NSAIDs; benign
  • Stress fracture — activity-related, recent change in loading

First-line tests for unexplained localised bone pain: X-ray of the site plus FBC, U&E, bone profile (calcium, phosphate, ALP), ESR/PV, CRP; protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains if >50 or unexplained; PSA in men where metastasis is considered; vitamin D if osteomalacia is possible.

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care management
accordion_sections.html:
• Any suspicious soft tissue lump → urgent ultrasound (request as urgent, noting ?sarcoma).
  • Unexplained localised bone pain → X-ray plus first-line bloods (see Assessment) — the bloods pick up the sarcoma mimics (myeloma, Paget's, metastasis, infection). If the X-ray is abnormal or pain persists despite a normal film, escalate — do not simply reassure on a single normal X-ray.
  • Do not excise or biopsy suspicious lumps in primary care (including 'lipomata' >5 cm or deep) — unplanned excision compromises definitive treatment.
  • Clinically obvious benign lesions (small, superficial, soft, mobile, stable): safety-net with instructions to return if growing, painful or changing.

accordion_sections.heading: Who to refer
accordion_sections.html:
Urgent suspicion of cancer (sarcoma pathway)

  • Ultrasound suspicious of sarcoma, or uncertain and clinical concern persists
  • Soft tissue lump >5 cm, deep, growing, painful or recurrent — refer in parallel with imaging if concern is high
  • X-ray suggesting possible bone sarcoma (destruction, periosteal reaction, soft tissue extension) — urgent referral/discussion; biopsy only at the specialist centre
  • Pathological fracture

Include in referral: duration and growth rate, size and depth, pain, previous excisions with histology, imaging reports, relevant history (radiotherapy, neurofibromatosis, retinoblastoma).

accordion_sections.heading: Who not to refer
accordion_sections.html:
• Small (<5 cm), superficial, soft, mobile, stable, painless lumps with benign characteristics — safety-net and review.
  • Classic wrist/hand ganglia — see the hand ganglion pathway.
  • Clinically typical sebaceous cysts and skin lesions — dermatology/minor surgery routes as appropriate.
  • Longstanding (>1 year), completely stable, asymptomatic lumps with benign imaging.
